title: Why Construction Firms Still Can't Escape Paper, and What It Costs Them
htmlTitle: Why Construction Firms Still Can't Escape Paper
author: Van Ausdall & Farrar
featuredImageAlt: Toy bulldozer beside a model house on a wooden desk
teaser: Construction still runs on paper. See what plan sets, submittals, change orders, and closeout binders cost firms, and how a hybrid workflow cuts the waste.
metaDescription: Construction still runs on paper. See what plan sets, submittals, change orders, and closeout binders cost firms, and how a hybrid workflow cuts the waste.
bodyHtml:
Construction has adopted more software than almost any other trade. Project management platforms, digital plan rooms, scheduling tools, field apps, and cloud file storage are standard at mid-sized firms. Yet the job trailer still has a printer, the closeout binder still gets assembled by hand, and a superintendent still carries a rolled set of drawings to a meeting.

That is not evidence that construction is behind. It is evidence that paper survives at the interfaces: between the owner and the contractor, between the contractor and the subcontractor, between the office and the field, and between the project and the lawyer, lender, or inspector who needs a record. Software has replaced the filing cabinet. It has not replaced the handoff.

Where Paper Still Enters a Project

Walk a project from award to closeout and the paper entry points are predictable:

  • Design and permitting: stamped plan sets, permit submissions, and revision sets that must match the authority having jurisdiction
  • Procurement: submittals, shop drawings, product data, samples, and approval stamps
  • Field operations: daily logs, safety checklists, job hazard analyses, inspection reports, punch lists, and delivery tickets
  • Commercial: contracts, change orders, lien waivers, pay applications, and certified payroll
  • Closeout: as-builts, O&M manuals, warranties, training records, and attestations assembled into binders

Even where the project team works digitally, many of these arrive as scans, photos, or PDFs from a partner who does not. The document is digital in one system and paper in another, and someone is paid to move it between the two.

The Direct Costs Are Easy to See

Plan printing is the visible line item. A full set can run hundreds of pages, and each revision means another round of printing and distribution. Large-format output, binding, and delivery add up quickly, especially on projects with frequent addenda. Firms often know the cost of a set but not the annual cost of all sets, all revisions, and all copies distributed to the field and to trade partners.

Then come the supporting costs:

  • Courier and hand delivery for signed documents and plan sets
  • Offsite storage and retrieval for closed projects
  • Jobsite printers, toner, service, and the staff time to keep them running
  • Scanning labor, overtime, and temporary help during closeout
  • Duplicate systems: the project management platform plus the shared drive plus the paper file

The Indirect Costs Are Larger

The expensive part of paper is not the paper. It is what happens when the document is wrong, missing, or in the wrong hands.

Version risk. A crew working from a superseded drawing can install the wrong thing, demolish the wrong wall, or order the wrong material. The rework cost dwarfs the printing cost, and it usually lands on the contractor even when the revision was issued weeks earlier.

Claims and delays. A missing daily log, an unsigned change order, or a delivery ticket that cannot be found weakens a claim or a defense at exactly the moment it matters. Construction disputes are won with records, and records that live in a truck, a trailer, or a former employee's filing cabinet are not reliable records.

Search time. Project managers and superintendents spend hours looking for documents that should take seconds to retrieve. Multiply that across a company and it becomes a payroll line item nobody budgeted for.

Closeout margin. Closeout is often the least profitable phase because it is compressed at the end. Assembling binders by hand, chasing missing warranties, and re-scanning documents that were already scanned once is pure margin loss.

Audit, legal, and insurance exposure. When a lender, insurer, auditor, or attorney asks for a project record, a paper archive answers slowly and incompletely. Digital records with an audit trail answer in minutes.

Disaster and loss. Paper stored in a trailer, a basement, or a storage unit is vulnerable to water, fire, pests, and simple misplacement. A single loss can erase years of project history.

Why the Digital Tools Have Not Replaced It

The persistence of paper is not a training problem. It is a structural one.

Legal and contractual requirements. Some documents still require wet signatures, notarization, or stamped and sealed sets. Permit offices and public agencies often set their own submission rules. A contractor cannot decide unilaterally to stop producing paper when the owner's contract requires it.

Partners at different maturity levels. A general contractor may run a sophisticated platform while a small specialty subcontractor works from email and a phone. The general contractor cannot force every partner onto its system, so the paper or PDF handoff survives as the common denominator.

Field conditions. Jobsite connectivity is better than it was, but it is still not universal. Mud, gloves, weather, and long days make a tablet less reliable than a printed set in some conditions. Paper works when the network does not.

Liability culture. Paper feels defensible. A signed, stamped, physically present document is easy to explain to an owner, an inspector, or a jury. Digital records feel less concrete even when they are more complete.

Duplication instead of replacement. Many firms added software without removing the old process. The document now exists in the platform, in email, on a shared drive, and in a binder. That is not digitization. It is the same paper process with more copies.

The Real Cost Is Rehandling

Every time a document changes hands, someone touches it again. Print, sign, scan, rename, email, file, retrieve, copy, distribute. The paper itself is cheap. The handling is expensive, and it multiplies with every additional copy and every additional party.

Scanning alone does not fix this. A PDF in a shared folder is a filing cabinet with a search box. The cost only drops when the document arrives in a system that expects it: indexed by project and type, versioned, permissioned, and attached to the workflow that needs it.

What a Workable Hybrid Looks Like

The goal is not zero paper. The goal is zero rehandling of documents that did not need to be paper in the first place. A realistic model has five parts:

  1. Capture at intake. Scan incoming paper once, with index fields for project, document type, phase, and date. Do not scan to a generic folder and promise to organize it later.
  2. One source of truth. A document management system with version control, permissions, and an audit trail. The platform can remain the project system of record; the document system holds the controlled record.
  3. Standard naming and structure. Every project uses the same document types and folder structure, so a new hire can find a submittal without asking a coworker.
  4. Digital signatures and forms where accepted. Use them for internal approvals, submittals, and change order routing, while keeping wet-ink processes where the contract or agency requires them.
  5. Managed output for the rest. Managed print services keeps jobsite and office printers supplied and serviced. Production print handles large plan sets and finishing when a project still needs paper. Document conversion clears the backfile and converts closeout binders into searchable records.

The workflow layer matters as much as the storage layer. Routing submittals, change orders, and pay applications through business process solutions removes the email chain that currently decides who approves what, and it leaves a record of the decision that a paper file never had.

Start With One Project

Do not begin with a company-wide platform decision. Pick one active project and measure four things: the cost of a full plan set through every revision, the hours spent assembling the closeout binder, the number of times a document is handled before it reaches its final home, and the storage cost of the closed project.

Those four numbers usually justify the first fix on their own. Then fix intake first, because the cheapest moment to add structure is when the document enters the building and someone still knows what it is.

Construction will keep some paper for a long time. The firms that control the cost are not the ones that eliminate every sheet. They are the ones that stop printing, scanning, filing, and searching for the same document four times. If you want a straight read on where your project records are costing you, start a conversation with our team.

title: In-House vs. Outsourced Production Print: Where the Break-Even Actually Is
htmlTitle: Production Print Break-Even: In-House vs. Outsourced
author: Van Ausdall & Farrar
featuredImageAlt: Two coworkers reviewing printed pages at a multifunction printer in an office
teaser: Where does in-house production print actually beat outsourcing? A practical break-even model covering fixed costs, click charges, labor, and monthly volume.
metaDescription: Where does in-house production print actually beat outsourcing? A practical break-even model covering fixed costs, click charges, labor, and monthly volume.
bodyHtml:
The production print decision usually gets framed as a binary. Buy a press, or send the work out. Most organizations that get this right do both, and the useful question is not which side wins. It is which job families belong on which side, at what monthly volume.

That question has an answer, and the answer is arithmetic. It is not a matter of taste, and it is not settled by a vendor's sample kit. Once you put the fixed costs and the variable costs in the right buckets, the break-even volume falls out of the model. The hard part is being honest about what goes in each bucket.

The Break-Even Is a Volume Calculation

Outsourcing turns print into a variable cost. You pay per job, and you pay nothing when the work does not exist. In-house printing turns most of the cost into a fixed monthly obligation: the lease, the service contract, the software, the floor space, and the operator. Those costs arrive whether the press runs or not.

That gives a simple formula:

Break-even volume = fixed monthly cost / (outsourced price per side - in-house variable cost per side)

Run below that volume and outsourcing is cheaper on cash. Run above it and the fixed investment is being used hard enough to pay for itself. The number is not permanent. A lease renewal, a click tier change, a wage increase, or a shift in job mix moves it.

What Belongs on the Fixed Side

The most common mistake is comparing an in-house click rate to an outsourced price per sheet. Click rate is not your cost. It is one line item. The fixed side usually includes:

  • Equipment lease or purchase, including the press, front end, and finishing
  • Service and parts, whether bundled or separate
  • Minimum click or subscription commitments
  • Workflow software: color management, imposition, and a web-to-print storefront
  • Floor space, power, and cooling, which production devices consume in volume
  • Operator labor, plus a trained backup, plus benefits
  • Supplies not included in the click charge: paper, toner, staples, coils, binders
  • Setup waste, spoilage, and reprints
  • Administration and integration with the systems that send work to the press

Labor deserves particular care. A half-time operator is still a headcount cost, and the backup who can run the press during vacation is either trained or a production risk. If existing staff absorb the work without adding hours, say so explicitly in the model. If they do not, the fully loaded cost belongs on the fixed side.

What Belongs on the Variable Side

On the in-house side, variable cost per side is mostly paper plus click. On the outsourced side, the comparison must be like for like: same stock, same finishing, same turnaround, same delivery. The outsourced unit price should include file preparation, delivery, and the reprint policy, because those are real costs that show up eventually.

Compare at the job level, not the catalog level. A quoted price for a long run on house stock is not comparable to a short run on a customer's specialty paper with binding and a next-day deadline. The more the job differs from the vendor's standard workflow, the more the quoted price will move once the details are known.

A Worked Example

Use illustrative numbers to see how the model behaves, then substitute your own lease, click tiers, and payroll.

  • Fixed monthly cost: $6,300 (equipment, software, space, and a part-time operator)
  • In-house variable cost: $0.10 per side (paper plus click)
  • Outsourced all-in price: $0.28 per side
  • Contribution per side: $0.18

Break-even volume is $6,300 divided by $0.18, or 35,000 sides per month. That is 17,500 sheets printed double-sided, or roughly 1,590 sides on each of 22 working days. At that volume the press is occupied for a meaningful part of every shift. Below it, the organization is paying for capacity it does not use. Above it, the in-house cost per side keeps falling as the fixed cost spreads across more work.

If your operation prints 12,000 sides a month, the model says keep outsourcing unless one of the non-financial factors below is decisive. At 60,000 sides a month, the same model says the fixed investment is doing its job, and the next question is how to keep utilization high.

Four Things That Move the Break-Even

1. Utilization and labor flexibility. A press that also produces variable data jobs, booklets, and customer-facing material throughout the week is a different asset than one that runs two days a month. If the operator can be redeployed during slow periods, the true fixed cost is lower. If the operator is dedicated and idle, the break-even rises.

2. Spoilage, downtime, and reprints. Every in-house reprint consumes clicks, paper, and labor that the quote did not include. Outsourcing passes production risk to the vendor, but rush fees and missed deadlines can cost more than the reprint itself. Track reprint rates for both sides instead of assuming one is cleaner.

3. Job mix. Short runs, variable data, frequent revisions, confidential files, and same-day turnaround generally favor in-house. Long runs, offset work, specialty stocks, perfect binding, and large format generally favor outsourcing. A single monthly volume total hides this. A job-family breakdown does not.

4. Capital and cash flow. An outsourced job costs money when it is produced. A press costs money at signing, whether or not the work materializes. Organizations with tight cash flow should discount the in-house case accordingly, even if the long-run unit economics look favorable.

The Hidden Cost of Sending Everything Out

Outsourcing has costs that do not appear on the invoice: transit time, revision cycles, file preparation, delivery windows, and the loss of control over a rush job. For a sales proposal that changes at 4 p.m., a next-day vendor cutoff is a business constraint, not just a line item. For a confidential document, sending files to an outside shop adds a data handling question.

In-house has hidden costs too. Operator turnover, training, maintenance windows, and equipment obsolescence are easy to underestimate at the start of a lease. The model is only useful if both sides carry their real costs, not just the visible ones.

A Decision Rule That Holds Up

Segment the work instead of deciding for the whole print operation. A practical split looks like this:

  • Keep in-house: short runs, variable data, frequent revisions, confidential work, and jobs with same-day or next-day deadlines
  • Keep outsourced: long runs, offset work, specialty finishing, large format, and overflow during peak periods
  • Review every six to twelve months: volume and job mix change, and lease terms eventually expire
  • Do not size the fixed cost to the peak: buy for the baseline and keep a reliable overflow path for the rest

That last point is where many in-house business cases fail. The press is purchased for the busiest month and then sits idle for the other eleven. A hybrid model avoids the problem by keeping the base volume in-house and routing the exceptions out.

Where Hybrid Wins

A hybrid setup lets each side do what it is good at. The in-house press handles fast, variable, confidential work. An outside partner handles long runs, offset, specialty finishing, and overflow. The fixed investment stays aligned with baseline demand, and the organization keeps access to capabilities it could not justify buying outright.

Van Ausdall & Farrar's production print work covers the presses, finishing, media profiles, and workflow software that make an in-house operation efficient. Managed print services handles the office fleet, supplies, service, and reporting that keep day-to-day output predictable. When the lower-volume devices need attention, copy print solutions starts with the equipment already in place, and copier sales covers replacement decisions against real scan and print volume rather than a spec sheet.

The break-even is not a slogan and it is not a reason to avoid either option. It is a number you can calculate before the next lease, and it gives you a defensible answer when someone asks why half the work goes out while a press sits in the back room.

If the model is close, or if the assumptions are hard to pin down, start a conversation with our team. We will walk the fixed and variable sides with you and tell you where your volume actually lands.

title: IT Solutions for Healthcare: HIPAA Technical Safeguards
htmlTitle: IT Solutions for Healthcare: HIPAA Technical Safeguards
author: Van Ausdall & Farrar
featuredImageAlt: Mechanical gears interlocked with circuit board technology representing healthcare IT infrastructure
teaser: HIPAA technical safeguards explained for healthcare IT: access control, encryption, audit logging, and the print and scan devices that touch patient data.
metaDescription: HIPAA technical safeguards explained for healthcare IT: access control, encryption, audit logging, and the print and scan devices that touch patient data.
bodyHtml:
The HIPAA Security Rule divides its requirements into three categories: administrative, physical, and technical safeguards. Most healthcare organizations can produce a policy binder for the first two. The technical safeguards are the ones that live or die on your actual infrastructure, and they are the ones an auditor will ask a system administrator to demonstrate rather than describe.

For a practice, clinic, or hospital department, that distinction matters. A written policy that says ePHI is encrypted does not satisfy the standard if nobody can show where the encryption is enforced. Here is what the technical safeguards require, and where healthcare environments usually have gaps.

The Five Technical Standards

The Security Rule names five technical safeguard standards, each with implementation specifications marked either required or addressable:

  • Access control (164.312(a)): unique user identification, emergency access procedure, automatic logoff, encryption and decryption
  • Audit controls (164.312(b)): hardware, software, and procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in systems containing ePHI
  • Integrity (164.312(c)): protections against improper alteration or destruction of ePHI
  • Person or entity authentication (164.312(d)): verify that the person seeking access is who they claim to be
  • Transmission security (164.312(e)): integrity controls and encryption for ePHI in transit

Addressable does not mean optional. It means you either implement the specification or document why it is not reasonable and appropriate, and implement an equivalent alternative. Auditors read that documentation closely.

Access Control Is an Identity Problem

Unique user identification is the required floor, and shared logins are the most common place healthcare organizations fall below it. A nursing station account that six people use cannot produce a meaningful audit trail, which means the access control failure and the audit control failure are the same finding.

What a defensible implementation looks like:

  • Individual accounts tied to a directory, not local logins on each workstation
  • Role based access, so a scheduler and a clinician see different records
  • Multi-factor authentication on anything reachable from outside the building
  • Automatic logoff on clinical workstations, with a timeout short enough to survive a shift change
  • A documented break-glass procedure for emergencies, and a review of every use of it

The break-glass piece is where policy and practice usually diverge. Clinicians will find a way into the record during an emergency. The question is whether that access is designed in advance and logged, or improvised and invisible. This is also the layer where general network security work and HIPAA compliance stop being separate projects, because identity is the control both depend on.

Audit Controls: If You Cannot Show It, You Cannot Prove It

Audit controls are required, and they are the safeguard most often implemented as a logging setting nobody reads. Logs that exist but are never reviewed satisfy the letter of the standard and fail its purpose, because the point is detecting inappropriate access before a patient complaint arrives.

What to build:

  1. Centralize logs from the EHR, the directory, and the file shares holding ePHI into one searchable location
  2. Set retention that matches your state record retention requirement, not the default 30 days
  3. Alert on specific events: after-hours record access, bulk exports, terminated accounts still active, repeated failed logins
  4. Review access to VIP and employee records on a schedule, and keep the review

That last item is the one that turns a technical control into a document an auditor will accept.

The Devices Nobody Counts

This is the gap we see most often in healthcare environments, and it has nothing to do with the EHR. Patient information passes through a long tail of equipment that sits outside the clinical system and outside most IT inventories:

  • Multifunction printers and copiers, many with internal hard drives that store every job they process
  • Scanners that cache a document image before it reaches its destination
  • Fax servers and analog lines still carrying referrals and lab results
  • Dictation and transcription systems
  • Mobile devices and tablets used at the bedside

Each one can hold ePHI at rest with no encryption and no access control. A copier pulled off lease and returned with its drive intact is a breach waiting on a disclosure requirement. The fixes are straightforward once someone owns the device list:

  • Authenticated print release, so a job does not print until the badge or login appears at the machine
  • Authenticated scanning and secure firmware from the manufacturer
  • Encrypted drives, and documented sanitization before disposal or lease return
  • Every printer and scanner included in the risk analysis, not just the servers

Paper is the same problem in a slower form. Legacy records in a file room have no access log at all until they are digitized. That work is a document management and scanning project before it is a compliance project, and it is the part of HIPAA readiness that healthcare organizations can actually finish. One Indiana hospital needed 1.5 million patient records indexed and secured inside a 90 day window before the storage building came down, and you can read how that patient records scanning project ran.

Transmission Security and Business Associate Agreements

Encryption in transit is addressable, and in practice there is no reasonable alternative for ePHI. Email carrying patient information needs transport encryption at minimum, and a secure portal or encrypted message is the better answer. Remote access belongs on a VPN with MFA, never on a published desktop with a password.

The requirement that catches healthcare organizations off guard is the business associate agreement. Every vendor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits ePHI on your behalf needs a signed BAA, and that list is longer than most people expect:

  • Your cloud and hosting providers
  • The software behind your print fleet and its reporting
  • Your phone system vendor, if calls are recorded
  • Anything that stores or indexes patient documents
  • Your IT provider itself

If a vendor will not sign a BAA, that is your answer about whether the tool should touch patient data.

Start With the Risk Analysis

None of this works as a checklist applied from the outside. The Security Rule requires a risk analysis first, and failures to conduct one are among the most frequently cited findings in HIPAA enforcement. The analysis is what tells you which of the safeguards above are actually missing in your environment, as opposed to missing on paper.

That is the shape of managed IT services in a healthcare setting. It is not a different discipline from business IT. It is the same work held to a documented standard, with the device inventory and the audit trail to prove it.

If your organization has never had a technical safeguards review, or the last one predates a new EHR, a merged practice, or a fleet of printers you inherited, start there. See our healthcare technology solutions for the full picture of how we support Indiana providers across IT, print, communications, and records.

title: Business Technology Simplified: A Century of Innovation
htmlTitle: Business Technology Simplified: A Century of Innovation
author: Van Ausdall & Farrar
featuredImageAlt: Abstract visualization of a data stream representing a century of business technology
teaser: From Edison wax cylinders in 1914 to managed IT services in 2026: 112 years of business technology, and why simplification still wins for Indiana companies.
metaDescription: From Edison wax cylinders in 1914 to managed IT services in 2026: 112 years of business technology, and why simplification still wins for Indiana companies.
bodyHtml:
In 1914, Oscar K. Van Ausdall became an Edison Business Phonograph dealer for the state of Indiana. The product was a wax cylinder dictating machine, and the pitch was simple: speak, and the machine takes the words down. No shorthand, no stenographer, no waiting. A lawyer or a doctor could finish a letter without writing it.

One hundred and twelve years later, the hardware is unrecognizable and the pitch has not changed. Business technology still sells itself as the thing that removes a step. The difference is what happens after you buy it.

Every Wave Arrives as a Simplification

Walk through the last century of office technology and a pattern holds. Each wave lands as relief and settles into a new set of things to manage.

  • Dictation. Voice to paper without a second person in the room.
  • Copying and printing. Duplicate a document in-house instead of sending it out.
  • Business phone systems. Reach anyone directly, then route, queue, and record the calls.
  • Networks and servers. Share files and applications without carrying them between desks.
  • Cloud. Stop buying hardware and start renting capacity.
  • Security. The invoice for everything above.
  • AI. The newest one, and the fastest to arrive.

Every line on that list made a task easier. Every line also added a system that someone has to own, patch, budget for, and eventually replace. That is the trade nobody puts on the brochure.

Simpler to Buy Is Not Simpler to Run

Most technology is easy to purchase and hard to live with. The purchase decision takes a week. The consequences run for seven years. A fleet of printers nobody tracks drifts into a per-page cost twice what it should be. A phone system gets installed by one vendor and supported by nobody. A cloud migration moves the servers and leaves the identity model exactly where it was.

The cost of a hundred years of accumulation is not the hardware. It is the seams. The places where two systems meet and neither vendor owns the result.

This is where document management earns its keep. Paper that enters a system as a scan, gets indexed, and routes itself to the right queue never needs a person to walk it down a hallway. The work disappears before anyone has to think about it.

Why Complexity Came Back

A 1914 office had one machine. A 2026 office has a print fleet, an endpoint fleet, a phone platform, a cloud tenant, a backup target, a compliance obligation, and forty logins. Each arriving wave was reasonable on its own. Nobody chose the total.

The result is a stack of vendors, each excellent inside their lane:

  • The copier dealer who services the hardware
  • The phone vendor who handles dial tone
  • The IT provider who keeps the network and endpoints running
  • The print software company with its own support queue
  • The security tooling that reports findings nobody acts on

Five contracts, five phone numbers, and one business owner holding the bag when the copier will not scan to a folder on a server that a different company manages. None of those vendors did anything wrong. The structure guaranteed the outcome.

What Simplification Actually Means

Simplification is not fewer devices. It is fewer decisions landing on your desk, and one place to call when something breaks.

In practice that looks like three things.

One accountable partner across the stack. When the scanner, the network, and cloud solutions are all supported by the same team, the seam stops being a dispute and becomes a ticket. Companies in Indianapolis get the most value here because the layers were never separate to begin with.

Technology matched to the process, not the other way around. A phone platform should fit how your front desk actually answers calls. A document workflow should match how an invoice actually gets approved. When the tool arrives first, the process bends around it and nobody is better off.

An owner for the whole picture. Someone has to see the print fleet, the network, the endpoints, the data, and the security posture at the same time. That role is what managed IT services exists to fill, and it is the reason the model spread from enterprises down to businesses with twenty employees.

A Hundred Years, One Question

The Century Building office on Market Street is long gone. The 57,000 square foot building on 75th Street replaced it in 2006, and the phone system in that building routes calls that used to ring at a switchboard downtown. The wax cylinders are in a display case.

Four generations of the same business have watched the same cycle repeat: a new technology arrives, it simplifies one task, it complicates the environment, and someone has to make the whole thing manageable again. The tools change every decade. The question does not.

It is not “which technology should we buy.” It is “who makes this simple to run.” For a hundred and twelve years, that has been the job. See the full company history, or start with the part that changes your week.

If your technology stack has grown faster than the team supporting it, that is a solvable problem and a short conversation. Explore managed IT services from Van Ausdall & Farrar and we will show you what a single accountable partner looks like across your print, network, cloud, and security.

title: Print & Copy Solutions: Where Document Workflows Start
htmlTitle: Print & Copy Solutions: Where Document Workflows Start
author: Van Ausdall & Farrar
featuredImageAlt: Two colleagues reviewing a digital document workflow on a tablet with data overlays in the background
teaser: Your multifunction printer is the fastest place to capture a document. How print and copy solutions turn each scan into a routed, searchable workflow.
metaDescription: Your multifunction printer is the fastest place to capture a document. How print and copy solutions turn each scan into a routed, searchable workflow.
bodyHtml:
Ask someone where a document enters their business and they will say email. Walk the floor and you find a different answer. It is the device standing next to the copier, the one with the feeder on top that everyone walks past on the way to the break room.

That machine is the front door for paper. Invoices, signed contracts, intake forms, referral packets, proof of delivery, identification documents, purchase orders. Most of it arrives on paper, gets scanned at that device, and lands in a folder somewhere with a filename like scan0012.pdf. The capture step already happens. What is missing is everything after it.

The Device Everyone Walks Past

Print and copy equipment gets bought for output and judged on output. Pages per minute, cost per page, toner yield. But look at what the same device does on the input side:

  • It has a document feeder that can move dozens of pages a minute
  • It has a scanner with resolution far beyond what a phone camera produces
  • It has a touchscreen, which means it can ask a question at the moment of capture
  • It has a network connection and, on most business models, a hard drive and a processor

That is a capture station with a keyboard attached. Treated as a copier, it produces piles of unstructured images. Treated as the entry point to a workflow, it produces indexed documents that route themselves.

Why Capture at the Device Beats Capture Later

The cheapest moment to add structure to a document is the moment it enters the building. Someone is already holding it. The context is still available: which customer, which job, which department, which date.

Every step of delay strips information out. A box that sits for a month becomes a batch job where an operator guesses at index fields. A stack scanned to a folder becomes a hunt through search results. Re-handling is the expensive part of paper, not the paper itself, and it grows every time a document changes hands.

What Workflow Entry Actually Means

Four capabilities separate a scanner from a workflow entry point.

1. A destination that is a system, not a folder. Scanning to a shared drive moves paper into a filing cabinet with better search. Scanning into a system that expects a document type means the document arrives where the work happens, with a queue, a status, and a responsible person.

2. Indexing at the moment of capture. Barcodes, OCR, and form recognition let the device read a document and pull the fields that matter before a human touches it. Invoice number, account number, date, dollar amount. Structured data at intake is what makes the rest of the process automatable.

3. Routing with rules. An invoice over a threshold goes to a second approver. A document missing a signature goes to an exception queue instead of stalling silently. Rules applied at intake replace the email chain that currently decides those things by memory.

4. An audit trail with an identity attached. This is the piece most organizations skip, and it is the one that makes the others trustworthy. Authenticated scanning means the device knows who scanned the document and when. Without it, a digital record is harder to defend than a signed paper one, because nobody can say who handled it.

The Hardware Still Has to Be Right

None of the above works on equipment that jams, scans slowly, or sits in the wrong hallway. The unglamorous prerequisites matter more than they sound:

  • Scan speed and feeder capacity matched to real volume, not to the demo
  • Duplex scanning, because most incoming paper is two-sided
  • Devices placed where the paper actually arrives, not where the lease renewal was easiest
  • Reliable service, since a capture point that is down sends everyone back to the filing cabinet

This is where a real fleet conversation happens. Managed print services covers the supply, service, and reporting side of the fleet, which is what keeps scanners available. When the fleet itself needs replacing, copier sales covers device selection against actual scan and print volume rather than a spec sheet, and copier service and repair covers the downtime that quietly kills any capture initiative.

Where Paper Still Earns Its Place

Not every document should be captured and routed. The distinction is worth being honest about.

High volume, repetitive, rules-based documents are the best candidates: invoices, orders, delivery tickets, intake packets, timesheets, applications. They arrive constantly, they look the same, and a person adds no judgment by handling them.

Low volume, judgment-heavy documents are a different problem. A one-off contract with negotiated terms is read by a human either way. Capturing it is still worth doing for the record, but automating the decision around it is not.

Start with the pile that grows fastest and looks the same every time. That is where the return lives.

What It Looks Like in Practice

Accounts payable. Mail arrives, gets opened, and is scanned with a barcode or a form-recognition routine that pulls the invoice number and amount. The document routes to the right approver by amount and vendor, exceptions go to a queue instead of an inbox, and the record exists in document management with an audit trail attached before anyone has typed a number.

Client or patient intake. Front desk scans the completed packet at the device, the system indexes by name and date of birth, and the record attaches to the account. No refiling, no lost page, no re-keying three fields into a second system.

Operations paperwork. Delivery tickets, job sheets, and inspection forms captured at the point where the work happened, with GPS or job number captured alongside, so the document and the job stay linked. This is the territory of business process solutions, and it is where the scan stops being an image and starts being a record.

Start by Counting Paper, Not Devices

The useful first move is not a new machine. It is a week of watching what comes in and where it piles up. Count the document types, the volume, and how many times each one is handled before it reaches its final home. That number is usually startling, and it points directly at the one process worth fixing first.

If your multifunction devices are doing nothing but copying and printing, the fastest efficiency gain available is already sitting in the hallway. Our copy print solutions work starts with the devices you already own and the documents already moving through them.

title: Data Discovery and Classification: Find Your Sensitive Data
htmlTitle: Data Discovery and Classification: Find Your Sensitive Data
author: Van Ausdall & Farrar
featuredImageAlt: Isometric illustration of servers, laptops, and network devices linked by green data lines
teaser: Van Ausdall & Farrar expands data discovery and classification to show where sensitive data lives, who can access it, and how to cut compliance risk.
metaDescription: Van Ausdall & Farrar expands data discovery and classification to show where sensitive data lives, who can access it, and how to cut compliance risk.
bodyHtml:
Leading Managed Technology Services Provider (MTSP) Expands Data Discovery and Classification Solutions to Reduce Compliance and Cybersecurity Risk

INDIANAPOLIS, IN ‐ Van Ausdall & Farrar, Inc., a leading managed technology services provider (MTSP), has expanded its data discovery and classification solutions, designed to help customers identify sensitive information, reduce unnecessary exposure, and strengthen compliance. As businesses generate more data than they can track, most organizations have lost sight of what data they actually have, and who can access it.

The reality for many organizations is simple: data grows quietly over time. Employee and customer names, financial records, medical information, contracts, credentials, and internal communications accumulate across email systems, cloud storage platforms, CRM systems, laptops, SharePoint, OneDrive, Box, Salesforce, and local devices. Yet very few companies pause to ask a critical question: do we truly know where our sensitive data lives, and who can see it?

Why Discovery Comes First

Data classification begins with discovery, identifying which information exists across an organization's IT environment. From there, data is categorized by sensitivity level: public, internal, confidential, regulated, or highly restricted. You cannot protect what you have never inventoried, and you cannot classify a file you do not know exists.

This matters most in industries where regulatory oversight is strict and penalties for non-compliance are severe, healthcare, financial services, government, public safety, and criminal justice among them. Under HIPAA, for example, violations range from relatively minor fines in unavoidable situations to penalties exceeding $1 million in cases of willful negligence. If you work in one of those industries, our article on HIPAA technical safeguards covers where healthcare environments typically have gaps.

The One Percent Permission Problem

"Most users only need about one percent of the permissions they actually are granted," said Guillermo Fernandez, VCIO of Van Ausdall & Farrar, Inc. "But because data keeps growing and access is rarely reviewed, organizations end up exposing far more to potential threats than they realize."

These errors are rarely malicious. Companies prioritize collaboration and efficiency, and the default mindset is to grant broad access so work can move quickly. That is well-intentioned, and it creates unnecessary risk that compounds as data grows. A shared drive that made sense for six people still carries the same permissions when it holds contracts and payroll files.

The fix is the Principle of Least Privilege: granting access only to the people who genuinely need it. Applied consistently, it reduces exposure while leaving employees free to work, and it turns a vague sense of risk into a list of specific permissions you can justify to an auditor.

Where AI Raises the Stakes

Artificial intelligence tools operate on existing permissions. If an employee can reach sensitive information, AI can surface it instantly and in plain language. "Even though it may seem efficient to give AI access, do you want your staff to be able to ask AI how much the owner is being compensated?" commented Fernandez.

When access controls are not structured properly, sensitive information becomes searchable and visible when it should not be. Data discovery is what makes AI adoption safe rather than risky, because it establishes the permission boundaries AI tools inherit. Organizations that clean up permissions first get the productivity gains without the exposure.

What a Discovery and Classification Engagement Looks Like

Modern data discovery and classification provides structured visibility into your environment. The process identifies where sensitive data resides, evaluates who has access to it, and aligns permissions with regulatory and operational requirements:

  • Scan email systems, file shares, cloud storage, CRM platforms, endpoints, and local devices for sensitive data patterns
  • Classify what is found by sensitivity level, so effort goes to the records that carry real risk
  • Map access : which users, groups, and service accounts can reach each category of data
  • Remove or narrow excessive permissions, starting with the widest exposure
  • Establish review cadence, so permissions do not silently drift back to broad access

For most businesses, the findings are humbling in a useful way. Files holding financial records or credentials are frequently reachable by far more people than the work requires, and nobody intended it. Unstructured data, scanned documents, exports, and archived files on shared drives, is usually the largest source of surprises, which is why document management and discovery tend to go hand in hand.

"Our goal is to give organizations clarity and confidence," Fernandez concluded. "Once you know what data you have and who can access it, you can protect it properly, and that peace of mind is invaluable."

Data discovery and classification are not a one-time project. New data arrives daily, employees change roles, and permissions accumulate. Treated as an ongoing part of managed IT services, classification keeps your network security posture honest instead of theoretical, and gives you an answer the next time someone asks where your sensitive data actually lives.

To find out what is exposed in your environment and who can see it, start a conversation with our team.

title: Digital Transformation: What It Looks Like Mid-Market
htmlTitle: Digital Transformation: What It Looks Like Mid-Market
author: Van Ausdall & Farrar
featuredImageAlt: Data visualization dashboard showing business metrics used to track digital transformation progress
teaser: Most mid-market digital transformation is not a megaproject. It is a sequence of unglamorous fixes to paper, phones, print, and identity that nobody announces.
metaDescription: Most mid-market digital transformation is not a megaproject. It is a sequence of unglamorous fixes to paper, phones, print, and identity that nobody announces.
bodyHtml:
The phrase digital transformation arrives with a certain picture attached. A steering committee. A multi-year roadmap. A consulting engagement with a phase one. Most mid-market companies look at that picture, decide it is not for them, and conclude they are behind.

They are not behind. They are just reading the wrong description of the work. Transformation at a company with forty or four hundred employees does not look like a program. It looks like a list of specific annoyances that stop happening, one at a time, until the building runs differently than it did two years ago.

What It Actually Looks Like From Inside

Strip the term down and the changes are ordinary:

  • The invoice that stops getting printed, walked down a hall, signed, scanned, and emailed back
  • The front desk that stops writing messages on paper slips
  • The employee who leaves, and whose access is gone before lunch instead of sometime next month
  • The file room that stops growing because new records arrive digital and stay that way
  • The approval that stops living in an inbox and starts living in a queue with a status

None of those will make a press release. All of them change how much work a person can finish in a day. That is the entire return on the effort, multiplied across a staff.

The Megaproject Model Was Built for Somebody Else

Large-enterprise transformation assumes a dedicated team, a CIO with budget authority, and slack in the organization to absorb disruption. Mid-market businesses have none of those. The person running the project is usually also running operations, or finance, or both, and the business still has to ship on Monday.

That constraint is not a weakness. It is a filter. A business that cannot afford a two-year program is forced to pick changes that pay for themselves quickly, which is a better discipline than a roadmap that assumes the money arrives on schedule.

The Four Layers That Actually Need Attention

Mid-market environments tend to have the same four layers, and each one has a predictable weak point.

1. Identity and Access

This is the layer everything else depends on, and it is usually the weakest. Shared logins, local accounts on each workstation, offboarding that relies on someone remembering. You cannot automate an approval if the system cannot tell who approved it. Fix identity first and every later project gets easier, because access, audit trails, and sign-off all rest on it.

2. Paper and Records

A file room is a slow process made physical. Every document that lives only on paper costs search time, storage, and a compliance answer you cannot produce quickly. Moving records into document management is the least glamorous work on this list and often the one that removes the most friction, because the people looking for those documents are your most expensive employees.

3. Communication

How calls reach the right person, whether the front desk can see who is available, whether a remote employee is reachable on the same system as everyone else. Modern business phone systems handle the routing and the reporting, and the reporting is the part that turns a communication complaint into a number you can act on. Call volume by hour tells you when you are understaffed. Abandoned call rate tells you whether the queue design works.

4. Workflow

Approvals, intake, exceptions, and the handoffs between departments. This is where business process solutions apply, and it is the layer where the payoff is easiest to measure, because someone can count the hours a process used to consume.

Where Mid-Market Transformations Stall

Most of the failures we see share one of four causes.

A vendor per layer. The copier company, the phone company, and the IT provider each solve their slice. Nobody owns the handoff where a scan needs to land in a folder on a server managed by a third company. The structure guarantees the argument.

Starting with the tool. A platform gets purchased before anyone has written down the process it is supposed to improve. The tool then becomes a second way of doing the same work, running alongside the first.

No owner for the whole map. Someone has to see the print fleet, the network, the phones, the records, and the identity model at the same time. In mid-market companies that role often does not exist formally, which is the gap managed IT services fills.

Measuring the wrong thing. Counting licenses purchased, systems deployed, or projects closed tells you what you spent. The measure that matters is hours removed from a real person's week. If nobody can name the process that got faster, the project has not transformed anything yet.

Sequence Beats Scope

If you want a plan that survives contact with a busy quarter, order the work like this:

  1. Identity first. Individual accounts, multi-factor authentication, and an offboarding checklist that runs the same way every time. Everything downstream depends on it, and it is the control that security insurance questionnaires ask about.
  2. Consolidate what you already own. Most mid-market companies are paying for overlapping tools and support contracts. Finding the overlap costs nothing and funds the next step.
  3. Digitize the paper that slows people down. Start with the records that get searched most often, not the oldest box in the room.
  4. Automate the repetitive approvals. Pick processes that are rules-based and high volume. If a process needs judgment on every instance, automate the intake and leave the decision alone.
  5. Measure, then decide the next one. One process at a time, each with a number attached, beats a roadmap nobody reviews.

Three Questions That Filter Any Project

Before approving anything, ask:

  1. Which specific process changes, and who does it today?
  2. Who owns this after go-live, when the enthusiasm has worn off?
  3. How will we know in ninety days whether it worked?

A project that cannot answer all three is a purchase, not a transformation. There is nothing wrong with a purchase, as long as everyone is honest that that is what it is.

Start With the Assessment, Not the Platform

You cannot sequence work you have not inventoried. The useful first step is a straight read on what you own, what it costs, what depends on what, and which single change would remove the most friction for the least disruption. That is a short engagement, not a program.

Schedule a Technology Strength Assessment and we will walk your environment with you, then tell you which of the four layers to fix first and what it will take.

title: AI Voice Clones and Deepfake Fraud: A Defense Playbook
htmlTitle: AI Voice Clones and Deepfake Fraud: A Defense Playbook
author: Van Ausdall & Farrar
featuredImageAlt: Fishing hook over a credit card on a computer keyboard, representing payment phishing
teaser: Voice clones and deepfakes now target wire transfers at small companies. The verification habits and controls that stop AI-powered payment fraud.
metaDescription: Voice clones and deepfakes now target wire transfers at small companies. The verification habits and controls that stop AI-powered payment fraud.
bodyHtml:
For twenty years, the advice about a suspicious request was simple: if it feels wrong, call and confirm. That advice assumed a phone call could prove identity. It no longer can.

Voice cloning tools need only a short sample of someone speaking, and a sample is easy to get from a voicemail greeting, a conference recording, or a webinar. Video is no longer a guarantee either. Live calls can carry a fabricated face, which is why the requests that used to fail on a bad email now arrive with the chief executive's voice attached.

The target is rarely the technology department. It is whoever can move money: accounts payable, bookkeeping, a controller, an office manager who handles banking in a company without a finance team. The defenses are procedural as much as technical, and most of them cost nothing to put in place.

Why Payment Processes Are the Target

Fraud follows the shortest path to value, and in a small business that path runs through a wire transfer or an updated bank account number. AI did not create this fraud. It removed the tells that used to give it away.

Older business email compromise had a recognizable texture: awkward phrasing, a mismatched domain, an excuse for why the executive could not take a call. AI-generated messages are clean, correctly spelled, and consistent with how your company actually writes. Combined with details scraped from your website, social accounts, and a single compromised mailbox, the message looks like routine business.

Four variants are showing up in small and mid-sized organizations:

  • Cloned executive voice. Someone in finance gets a call or voicemail that sounds like the owner or CFO, urgent and slightly annoyed, asking for a payment to be pushed through before a deadline.
  • Live deepfake on video. A short video call with a familiar face establishes trust, then hands off to "a colleague" over email for the banking details, because the fabricated video is easier to sustain for a minute than for a meeting.
  • Vendor account change. A vendor's mailbox is compromised or impersonated, and the only change is a new remittance account. The invoice amounts stay normal.
  • Help desk impersonation. An attacker calls support posing as a traveling employee, using a cloned voice of a real manager, and asks for a multi-factor reset. One reset hands over a mailbox.

Every one of these depends on the same thing: a person making a decision inside a short window, on the strength of a voice, a face, or a lookalike domain.

Rule One: Verify Out of Band, Every Time

Verification has to happen on a channel the requester did not choose. If the request arrives by phone, confirm through a channel you already trust. If it arrives by email, confirm by calling a number from your own records.

The rule that carries the most weight is narrow and absolute: any change to payment instructions gets confirmed by calling a known contact at the vendor, at a number from the contract or the vendor master, never a number included in the request. That one control defeats most invoice fraud, including the AI-assisted kind, because the attacker cannot answer a phone that was already in your file.

Add a second rule for volume: no single person can both initiate and release a payment, and anything above a set threshold needs a second approval from someone who was not on the original thread. Fraud depends on a single point of trust. Two approvals remove it.

Rule Two: Never Approve on Voice or Video Alone

Teams that have adopted "the CEO can just call me" as a shortcut need to retire it. Announce the change now, before an incident, so declining a request does not feel like insubordination.

Practically, that means a written payment authorization procedure that names who can approve what, at which thresholds, and which channels count as valid. A phone call or a video meeting is a trigger to start verification, not the verification itself. Train the people who handle payments on this specific scenario, using your own executive names and a realistic script. Generic annual awareness modules do not prepare anyone for a familiar voice asking for something urgent.

Rule Three: Raise the Technical Cost

Procedures stop the attacks that reach a person. Technical controls stop the ones that never need to.

  • Enforce SPF, DKIM, and DMARC on your domain so attackers cannot send mail that passes as yours, and watch the reports for spoofing attempts
  • Tag external email so a message claiming to be from the next office is visibly from outside
  • Alert on mailbox rules that hide or forward messages, since a compromised mailbox usually sets one up
  • Require phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication for finance, email, and administrative accounts
  • Record change history on the vendor master and alert when banking details are edited
  • Give the help desk an identity verification script for password and MFA resets, and no exceptions to it

None of these are exotic. They are the same network security basics that stop ordinary phishing, pointed at a new pretext. The full set of quarterly tasks is in our October action plan for Cybersecurity Awareness Month.

What to Do When a Payment Already Went Out

Speed matters more than investigation. Call your bank immediately and request a recall of the wire, then notify your insurer under the cyber or crime policy, and preserve the evidence: headers, call records, and the messages themselves. In many cases a wire recalled within hours is recovered, and one recalled the next day is not.

Two details are worth setting up before you need them. Know which policy at your insurer covers social engineering fraud, because standard cyber policies often exclude it or sublimit it, and confirm your bank's recall process and cutoff times now rather than during an incident.

Where This Fits in the Bigger Picture

AI has not changed what attackers want. It has changed how convincing they are on the way to getting it, which shifts the burden onto verification habits, authorization rules, and the boring identity controls underneath them. Those are the parts a company can control.

That work is what managed IT services covers when a business has no security team of its own: enforcement of email authentication, MFA and help desk procedures, and alerting that catches the mailbox rule nobody remembers creating. If you are not sure where your exposure sits today, a cyber threat assessment will show you, including the payment process gaps that insurance questionnaires now ask about. Contact our team to get one scheduled.

title: Cybersecurity Awareness Month: A 30-Day Action Plan
htmlTitle: Cybersecurity Awareness Month: A 30-Day Action Plan
author: Van Ausdall & Farrar
featuredImageAlt: Hands typing on keyboards beneath glowing DATA BREACH text over binary code
teaser: A four-week plan for October: multi-factor authentication, patching, phishing drills, and a backup restore test that proves your defenses actually hold.
metaDescription: A four-week plan for October: multi-factor authentication, patching, phishing drills, and a backup restore test that proves your defenses actually hold.
bodyHtml:
October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month. For most small and mid-sized businesses it passes the way it always does: a vendor email, a poster in the break room, and nothing in the environment that actually changes. That is the wrong outcome for the cheapest month of security work on the calendar.

The patterns behind breaches at companies this size do not change much from year to year. Credentials that were stolen or reused, a device nobody patched, an employee who believed a convincing email, and a backup that turned out not to restore. None of that requires a security department to fix. It requires four weeks of attention and one person who owns the list.

Here is a 30-day plan for a company without a security team. One task per week, each one something you can verify, and each one producing a result you can hand to an auditor, an insurer, or a customer who sends a security questionnaire.

Week 1: Put Multi-Factor Authentication Where It Counts

If you do one thing in October, do this one. Stolen credentials are still the most common way an attacker gets in, and multi-factor authentication is the control that breaks it. A password that leaks in a breach somewhere else is useless to an attacker who cannot pass the second factor.

Do not try to cover every system in a week. Work in this order:

  1. Email, because it is the account everything else resets through
  2. Remote access, including VPN and any published desktop
  3. Finance and payroll systems, where the money moves
  4. Administrative accounts on your servers, network gear, and cloud consoles
  5. Line of business applications holding customer or patient data

Use an authenticator app or a hardware key. Text message codes are better than nothing, but they are the weakest form and are routinely defeated by SIM swapping and relay attacks. Expect a week of support tickets and a few people who lose a phone. Plan the help desk time rather than being surprised by it.

Week 2: Build the Device List, Then Patch It

You cannot patch what nobody has counted. Most organizations can name their servers and have no idea how many devices actually sit on the network. Start with an inventory, and include the equipment that never makes the IT spreadsheet:

  • Workstations and laptops, including the ones people bought themselves
  • Servers, physical and virtual
  • Firewalls, switches, and wireless access points
  • Multifunction printers and copiers, which run firmware and often hold a hard drive
  • Phone systems, cameras, and anything else with an IP address

Once the list exists, set a patch cadence you can keep: operating systems and browsers on automatic updates, servers and network gear on a monthly maintenance window, firmware checked quarterly. The exploitable vulnerabilities in most small business incidents were public for months before anyone used them. Good network security is less about exotic tools than about closing known holes on a schedule.

Week 3: Run a Phishing Drill, Then Train to the Result

Awareness training that everyone clicks through once a year does not change behavior. A simulated phishing email does, because it produces a number you can compare month over month.

Run a baseline test in week three and keep it fair. Use a template that looks like the real thing at your company: an invoice from a known vendor, a password expiry notice, a message that appears to come from a manager. Then train to what people actually missed rather than to a generic module.

Three things make the difference between a drill that helps and one that breeds resentment:

  • Tell people the program exists and that reporting is the goal, not a clean click rate
  • Give every mailbox a one-click report button, and thank the people who use it
  • Never punish someone who clicks. Punished employees hide the next mistake, and hiding is what turns an incident into a breach

Van Ausdall & Farrar offers free security awareness training and free security training tools you can run against your own staff this month at no cost.

Week 4: Restore a Backup on Purpose

An untested backup is a hope, not a control. The failure mode is consistent: the backup job reports success for two years, and on the day it matters, the restore fails halfway through. Ransomware operators count on exactly that.

Spend week four proving recovery works:

  1. Pick a real server or a real file share, and restore it to a lab or spare hardware
  2. Time the restore and write the number down, because that is your actual downtime
  3. Confirm at least one copy is offline or immutable, so an attacker with domain admin cannot encrypt it
  4. Check whether the last year of data is really in the backup, or only the last 30 days

If the restore fails, you have found a problem in October instead of on a Tuesday morning when production is down. That is a win, not a failure. Most organizations that recover quickly from ransomware got there by testing, and the ones that pay are usually the ones that never did.

The Other Eleven Months

The month ends and nothing you fixed stays fixed on its own. Access changes when people are hired and leave, new devices appear, and last year's clean phishing number drifts back up. What keeps the work from decaying is a regular review: who has access to what, what is unpatched, whether the backup still restores, and whether the alerting you pay for is being read by someone.

That is what managed IT services covers for companies without a security team of their own. Awareness month is a good prompt to start, but the value is in the twelve months that follow it.

If you want a starting point that tells you where your environment actually stands, a cyber threat assessment gives you the inventory, the gaps, and the priorities in one pass. Contact our team to schedule one this October.

title: Multi-Cloud vs. Hybrid Cloud: Choosing the Right Strategy
htmlTitle: Multi-Cloud vs. Hybrid Cloud: Choosing Your Strategy
author: Van Ausdall & Farrar
teaser: A multi-cloud strategy involves using cloud services from multiple public cloud providers simultaneously. Contact us today to learn more about your options.
metaDescription: A multi-cloud strategy involves using cloud services from multiple public cloud providers simultaneously. Contact us today to learn more about your options.
bodyHtml:
Understanding the Cloud Strategy Dilemma

Organizations increasingly face a critical decision: should they adopt a multi-cloud strategy, leverage a hybrid cloud approach, or implement some combination of both? With 92% of enterprises now using a multi-cloud strategy according to recent industry research, understanding the distinctions between these approaches has never been more important for business leaders.

The choice between multi-cloud and hybrid cloud isn't simply a technical decision - it directly impacts operational efficiency, cost management, data security, and business agility. Each approach serves different organizational needs, and selecting the wrong strategy can lead to unnecessary complexity, increased costs, and security vulnerabilities.

Defining Multi-Cloud and Hybrid Cloud

What Is Multi-Cloud?

A multi-cloud strategy involves using cloud services from multiple public cloud providers simultaneously. For example, an organization might use Amazon Web Services (AWS) for data analytics, Microsoft Azure for application development, and Google Cloud Platform for machine learning workloads. Each provider is selected based on their specific strengths for particular applications or services.

Key characteristics of multi-cloud include:

  • Multiple public cloud providers operating independently
  • Workloads distributed across different cloud platforms
  • Provider selection based on best-of-breed capabilities
  • Reduced vendor lock-in and increased negotiating power
  • Geographic distribution for compliance and performance optimization

What Is Hybrid Cloud?

A hybrid cloud architecture combines private cloud or on-premises infrastructure with public cloud services, creating an integrated environment where data and applications can move between private and public resources. This approach allows organizations to maintain sensitive workloads on-premises while leveraging public cloud resources for scalability and innovation.

Key characteristics of hybrid cloud include:

  • Integration between private (on-premises or hosted) and public cloud environments
  • Orchestration and management across both environments
  • Data and application portability between private and public resources
  • Flexibility to keep sensitive data on-premises while using cloud for burst capacity
  • Unified management and security policies across environments

Evaluating Your Workload Requirements

The right cloud strategy depends heavily on your specific workload characteristics and business requirements. Understanding these factors is essential before committing to either approach.

Data Sensitivity and Compliance Needs

Organizations in healthcare, financial services, and government sectors often face stringent regulatory requirements regarding data residency, privacy, and security. If your organization handles highly sensitive data subject to regulations like HIPAA, PCI DSS, or government compliance standards, a hybrid cloud approach may provide better control over where data resides and how it's protected.

However, if compliance requirements vary by workload or geographic region, a multi-cloud strategy might offer the flexibility to select cloud providers with specific certifications or regional data centers that meet your compliance needs.

Performance and Latency Requirements

Applications requiring low latency or high-performance computing may benefit from different cloud strategies. Multi-cloud allows you to position workloads in the cloud provider's data center closest to your users, optimizing performance globally. Hybrid cloud enables you to keep latency-sensitive applications on-premises while using public cloud for less time-critical workloads.

Scalability and Flexibility Needs

Consider how your workloads scale. Do you experience predictable seasonal spikes, unpredictable demand surges, or steady-state operations? Hybrid cloud excels at "cloud bursting" - maintaining baseline operations on-premises while automatically scaling to public cloud during peak demand periods. Multi-cloud provides redundancy and the ability to scale across multiple providers, offering protection against service outages and capacity limitations from a single provider.

Strategic Advantages of Multi-Cloud

Multi-cloud strategies offer several compelling benefits that make them attractive for many organizations:

Avoiding Vendor Lock-In

By distributing workloads across multiple cloud providers, organizations reduce dependence on any single vendor's pricing, technology roadmap, or service availability. This provides greater negotiating leverage and protection against vendor-specific outages or policy changes that could impact operations.

Best-of-Breed Approach

Different cloud providers excel in different areas. AWS offers the broadest range of services and global reach. Azure integrates seamlessly with Microsoft enterprise tools. Google Cloud Platform leads in data analytics and machine learning capabilities. A multi-cloud approach allows you to leverage each provider's strengths for specific workloads rather than settling for one provider's limitations across all use cases.

Geographic Distribution and Resilience

Multi-cloud enables true geographic diversity, reducing the risk of regional outages affecting all your operations. By distributing critical workloads across providers with different infrastructure footprints, you create architectural resilience that exceeds what's possible within a single cloud ecosystem.

Strategic Advantages of Hybrid Cloud

Hybrid cloud architectures provide their own set of powerful benefits for organizations with specific requirements:

Control and Security

Maintaining on-premises infrastructure gives organizations direct control over their most sensitive data and applications. This is particularly valuable for organizations in regulated industries or those with proprietary systems that can't easily migrate to public cloud. A well-designed hybrid cloud approach, supported by experienced managed IT services, provides the security of on-premises infrastructure with cloud scalability where appropriate.

Legacy System Integration

Many organizations operate legacy systems that are difficult or impossible to migrate to public cloud due to technical constraints, licensing restrictions, or business continuity risks. Hybrid cloud allows these systems to remain on-premises while modern applications leverage cloud capabilities, creating a bridge between legacy and modern architectures.

Cost Optimization

For workloads with consistent, predictable demand, maintaining on-premises infrastructure can be more cost-effective than paying for equivalent public cloud resources continuously. Hybrid cloud enables organizations to optimize costs by keeping steady-state workloads on-premises while using public cloud for variable demand, development environments, and new initiatives.

Making the Right Choice for Your Organization

Selecting between multi-cloud and hybrid cloud requires honest assessment of your organization's current state and future direction:

Questions to Guide Your Decision

  • What is your existing infrastructure investment? Organizations with significant on-premises infrastructure investments may benefit from hybrid cloud to maximize ROI on existing assets while gaining cloud capabilities.
  • What are your regulatory and compliance requirements? Highly regulated industries often require hybrid approaches for control and compliance, while organizations with less stringent requirements may prefer multi-cloud flexibility.
  • What is your team's cloud expertise? Managing multiple cloud providers requires diverse skills and sophisticated orchestration. Organizations with limited cloud expertise may find hybrid cloud easier to manage initially.
  • What are your application architectures? Cloud-native applications designed with microservices and containerization adapt well to multi-cloud. Legacy monolithic applications may require hybrid approaches.
  • What is your budget for cloud operations? Multi-cloud strategies require investment in cross-cloud management tools and expertise. Hybrid cloud requires maintaining on-premises infrastructure alongside cloud resources.

The Hybrid Multi-Cloud Approach

Increasingly, organizations are recognizing that the choice isn't binary. A hybrid multi-cloud strategy combines elements of both approaches - maintaining on-premises infrastructure for specific workloads while leveraging multiple public cloud providers for different applications and services. This provides maximum flexibility but also introduces significant complexity in management, security, and integration.

Implementation Considerations

Regardless of which strategy you choose, successful implementation requires careful planning and the right expertise:

Management and Orchestration

Both multi-cloud and hybrid cloud environments require sophisticated management tools to maintain visibility, control costs, and ensure security across distributed resources. Implementing comprehensive cloud solutions with unified management capabilities is essential for operational efficiency.

Security and Compliance

Distributed cloud environments create expanded attack surfaces and compliance complexities. Organizations need consistent security policies, identity and access management, and data security practices across all cloud and on-premises resources. Regular security assessments and continuous monitoring are non-negotiable.

Network Connectivity

Hybrid cloud requires reliable, high-bandwidth connectivity between on-premises and cloud resources. Multi-cloud may require connectivity between different cloud providers for integrated operations. Network architecture becomes a critical success factor for both strategies.

Skills and Training

Your IT team needs appropriate skills to manage your chosen cloud strategy. Multi-cloud requires expertise across multiple provider platforms. Hybrid cloud demands skills in both traditional infrastructure and cloud technologies. Investing in training or partnering with experienced providers is essential for long-term success.

Moving Forward With Confidence

The choice between multi-cloud and hybrid cloud isn't about selecting the "better" option - it's about identifying which approach best aligns with your workload requirements, business objectives, and organizational capabilities. Many successful organizations use hybrid approaches initially to modernize incrementally while maintaining control, then evolve toward multi-cloud as applications become cloud-native and teams develop broader expertise.

The key is starting with a clear understanding of your current state, defining your desired future state, and creating a realistic roadmap that accounts for technical requirements, budget constraints, and organizational readiness. With over a century of experience helping organizations navigate technology transitions, Van Ausdall & Farrar understands that successful cloud strategies balance innovation with practicality.

Whether you're just beginning your cloud journey or looking to optimize an existing cloud environment, the right strategy depends on your unique circumstances. Contact our team to discuss how we can help you evaluate your options and implement a cloud strategy that delivers real business value while managing complexity and risk effectively.
