bodyHtml:
Leading Managed Technology Services Provider (MTSP) Provides Innovative Technology to Transform and Enhance Processes

INDIANAPOLIS, IN - Van Ausdall & Farrar, Inc. a leading managed technology services provider (MTSP), announced the launch of a new AI-powered automation solution designed to help small and midsized businesses complete repetitive back-office work faster, improve accuracy, and create more efficient workflows without requiring employees to become software developers.

Most businesses have routine processes that consume far more time than owners realize. For example, accounting teams compare invoices with billing records. Managers assemble information from several data systems to create reports. Employees copy data between spreadsheets, prepare recurring documents, follow up on incomplete forms, and manually check whether information matches. Individually, these assignments may appear minor. However, across an entire organization, these innocent tasks, can absorb hundreds of employee hours while creating opportunities for mistakes, delays, and inconsistent results. Van Ausdall & Farrar, Inc. is using AI workflow automation to help businesses recapture lost hours, increase accuracy and free up employees to work on higher-level, creative work.

"Most businesses do not need another piece of software that gives their employees more work," said Guillermo Fernandez, VCIO at Van Ausdall & Farrar, Inc. "They need technology that can take a repetitive process off someone's desk and complete it accurately. The purpose of this solution is essentially to give everyone on a team a software developer and AI automation expert, so they have even more resources to perform. Once they're not mired in the mundane, they can be strategic and help propel your organization to new heights. While many AI tools are incredibly complex, we've put together a simple solution."

Unlike traditional chatbots that explain how to perform a task, Van Ausdall & Farrar, Inc's new AI Workflow Automation technology can carry out a series of approved steps and deliver a finished result. For example, imagine a company that spends several hours every month comparing service records, customer invoices, and accounting data. An employee may need to export information from several platforms, review rows individually, identify discrepancies, and prepare a summary for management. But with AI automation, the employee can design a repeatable process that collects the approved information, checks for inconsistencies, organizes the results, and produces a report for review on a recurring basis.

"Your team should be designing processes and delegating repetitive execution to AI," added Fernandez. "The goal is not to automate everything simply because we can. The goal is to identify work that repeatedly consumes valuable employee time and ask whether technology can handle the routine portion more efficiently. That gives people more time to solve problems, serve customers, and perform the work that requires their judgment or is more personally fulfilling."

Rather than asking owners to select tools, build complicated integrations, or learn technical systems, Van Ausdall & Farrar, Inc. can help identify a useful process, define the desired outcome, and design an automation around the way the company already operates. This allows businesses to begin with a specific problem instead of purchasing random AI technology without a clear, practical use for it.

Human oversight remains an important part of the process. Employees and managers can review completed work, confirm accuracy, and maintain control over decisions that affect customers, finances, employees, or business operations. This combination of automation and human judgment enables businesses to increase speed without blindly handing important responsibilities to a machine. Effectively, everyone on a team is now in leadership and has their own direct AI reports to manage.

"AI should not be a science project," Fernandez concluded. "It should solve a real business problem. When we meet with you and can help you turn hours of repetitive work into a process that is completed quickly and consistently, it gives the organization additional capacity without simply asking employees to work harder."

title: AI Integrations: Transforming Business Operations in 2026
htmlTitle: AI Integrations: Transforming Business Operations Now
author: Van Ausdall & Farrar
teaser: Artificial intelligence has moved beyond experimental technology to become a fundamental component of competitive business operations. Contact us to learn more.
metaDescription: Artificial intelligence has moved beyond experimental technology to become a fundamental component of competitive business operations. Contact us to learn more.
bodyHtml:
The Business Case for AI Integration

Artificial intelligence has moved beyond experimental technology to become a fundamental component of competitive business operations. Organizations across industries are discovering that strategic AI integrations deliver measurable improvements in efficiency, accuracy, and customer satisfaction. For companies ready to embrace this transformation, understanding where and how to implement AI is the key to unlocking its full potential.

At Van Ausdall & Farrar, we've witnessed firsthand how businesses throughout the Midwest are leveraging AI to solve real-world challenges. From automating routine tasks to enhancing decision-making capabilities, AI integrations are no longer optional for organizations seeking to maintain their competitive edge. The question isn't whether to integrate AI, but rather how to do so strategically and effectively.

Understanding Modern AI Integration Opportunities

AI integration encompasses a broad spectrum of applications, each designed to address specific business needs. The most successful implementations begin with identifying pain points and matching them with appropriate AI solutions.

Document Processing and Data Extraction

One of the most impactful areas for AI integration is automated forms processing and document management. Traditional document handling requires significant manual effort, introducing opportunities for errors and delays. AI-powered systems can now extract data from invoices, contracts, and forms with remarkable accuracy, processing hundreds of documents in the time it would take a human to handle just one.

Healthcare organizations, for instance, are using AI to process patient intake forms and insurance documents, reducing administrative burden while improving data accuracy. Financial services firms leverage AI to extract critical information from loan applications and compliance documents, accelerating approval processes while maintaining regulatory standards.

Intelligent Communication Systems

Modern communication infrastructure benefits tremendously from AI integration. Cloud-based phone systems now incorporate AI-driven features such as intelligent call routing, voice analytics, and automated transcription services. These capabilities transform how businesses interact with customers and how teams collaborate internally.

Call centers equipped with AI can analyze customer sentiment in real-time, routing calls to the most appropriate agents based on detected emotions and intent. Transcription services powered by AI create searchable records of conversations, enabling better training, compliance monitoring, and customer service quality assurance.

Predictive Maintenance and IT Operations

For organizations relying on complex technology infrastructure, AI-powered predictive maintenance represents a significant advancement. Rather than waiting for equipment failures or following rigid maintenance schedules, AI systems analyze patterns and predict when issues are likely to occur.

Managed IT services increasingly incorporate AI to monitor network performance, identify security threats, and optimize system resources. This proactive approach reduces downtime, extends equipment lifespan, and allows IT teams to focus on strategic initiatives rather than reactive troubleshooting.

Strategic Implementation: Getting AI Integration Right

Successful AI integration requires thoughtful planning and execution. Organizations that rush into implementation without proper strategy often encounter disappointing results. Here's how to approach AI integration strategically:

Start with Clear Objectives

Define specific, measurable goals for your AI integration. Rather than implementing AI for its own sake, identify concrete business outcomes you want to achieve. Are you looking to reduce processing time by 50%? Improve customer satisfaction scores? Decrease operational costs? Clear objectives guide technology selection and provide benchmarks for measuring success.

Assess Data Readiness

AI systems are only as effective as the data they can access. Before implementing AI solutions, evaluate your data infrastructure. Is your data organized, accessible, and of sufficient quality? Many organizations discover that their data exists in silos across disconnected systems, requiring integration work before AI can deliver value.

Document management solutions create the foundation for successful AI integration by organizing and digitizing information, making it accessible for AI processing.

Choose the Right Integration Approach

AI integration can take several forms, from pre-built solutions to custom developments. For most businesses, starting with proven, industry-specific AI applications offers the fastest path to value. These solutions address common challenges and require less customization than building AI systems from scratch.

Consider cloud-based AI services that integrate with your existing systems. This approach reduces infrastructure investment and allows you to scale AI capabilities as your needs evolve.

Industry-Specific AI Applications

Different industries benefit from AI integration in unique ways, tailored to their specific operational challenges and opportunities.

Healthcare

Healthcare organizations are using AI to improve patient outcomes and operational efficiency. Beyond document processing, AI helps with medical imaging analysis, patient scheduling optimization, and clinical decision support. Voice recognition and transcription services allow physicians to focus on patient care rather than documentation.

Financial Services

Banks and insurance companies leverage AI for fraud detection, risk assessment, and customer service automation. Chatbots handle routine inquiries, while AI-powered analytics identify patterns that human analysts might miss. Compliance monitoring systems use AI to flag suspicious transactions and ensure regulatory adherence.

Manufacturing and Logistics

Manufacturing operations benefit from AI-driven quality control, supply chain optimization, and predictive maintenance. Computer vision systems inspect products for defects with greater consistency than human inspectors. AI algorithms optimize inventory levels and predict demand fluctuations, reducing waste and improving delivery times.

Education

Educational institutions are implementing AI for personalized learning experiences, administrative automation, and student support services. AI-powered systems can identify students at risk of falling behind and recommend interventions, while automating routine administrative tasks frees staff to focus on student engagement.

Overcoming Common Implementation Challenges

While AI integration offers tremendous benefits, organizations often encounter challenges during implementation. Understanding these potential obstacles helps you prepare and navigate them effectively.

Data Privacy and Security Concerns

AI systems require access to business data, raising legitimate concerns about privacy and security. Address these concerns by implementing robust cyber security solutions and ensuring AI vendors comply with relevant regulations. Establish clear data governance policies that define what data AI systems can access and how it will be used.

Change Management and User Adoption

Technology implementation succeeds or fails based on user adoption. Employees may resist AI integration due to concerns about job displacement or skepticism about the technology's effectiveness. Address these concerns through transparent communication, comprehensive training, and involving users in the implementation process.

Demonstrate AI as a tool that augments human capabilities rather than replaces them. When employees see AI handling tedious, repetitive tasks and freeing them for more meaningful work, resistance typically diminishes.

Integration with Legacy Systems

Many organizations operate legacy systems that weren't designed with AI integration in mind. Rather than replacing entire systems, an expensive and risky proposition, look for AI solutions that can interface with existing infrastructure through APIs and integration platforms.

Measuring ROI and Long-Term Success

Quantifying the return on AI investment requires tracking both tangible and intangible benefits. Hard metrics might include processing time reductions, error rate decreases, and cost savings. Softer benefits include improved employee satisfaction, better customer experiences, and enhanced decision-making capabilities.

Establish baseline measurements before implementation and track metrics consistently. Most organizations see ROI within 12-18 months for properly implemented AI solutions, with benefits accelerating as systems learn and improve over time.

The Future of AI Integration

AI technology continues evolving rapidly, with new capabilities emerging regularly. Organizations that establish AI integration capabilities now position themselves to leverage future innovations more easily. The infrastructure, skills, and organizational understanding developed through initial AI projects create a foundation for ongoing digital transformation.

Looking ahead, expect AI to become increasingly accessible and powerful. Natural language processing will enable more intuitive interactions with business systems. Computer vision will expand into new applications. AI will increasingly work alongside humans in augmented intelligence scenarios, combining artificial and human intelligence for optimal outcomes.

Taking the Next Step

AI integration represents a significant opportunity for businesses ready to embrace transformation. Success requires strategic thinking, careful planning, and partnership with experienced technology providers who understand both AI capabilities and practical business applications.

At Van Ausdall & Farrar, we help organizations throughout the Midwest navigate AI integration successfully. Our team brings over a century of technology expertise combined with deep understanding of AI's practical applications across industries. We work with you to identify opportunities, develop implementation strategies, and ensure your AI investments deliver measurable results.

Whether you're taking your first steps with AI or looking to expand existing capabilities, contact us to discuss how AI integration can transform your operations. Let's explore how artificial intelligence can address your specific business challenges and position your organization for continued success in an increasingly AI-driven business environment.

title: Data Quality vs. Data Quantity: Why More Isn't Always Better
htmlTitle: Data Quality vs. Data Quantity: Which Matters More?
author: Van Ausdall & Farrar
teaser: Business leaders today face a counterintuitive challenge: despite collecting more data than ever before, many organizations struggle to make better decisions.
metaDescription: Business leaders today face a counterintuitive challenge: despite collecting more data than ever before, many organizations struggle to make better decisions.
bodyHtml:
The Data Overload Paradox

Business leaders today face a counterintuitive challenge: despite collecting more data than ever before, many organizations struggle to make better decisions. The problem isn't a lack of information - it's the overwhelming abundance of it. Companies generate approximately 2.5 quintillion bytes of data daily, yet studies show that up to 73% of enterprise data goes unused for analytics.

This phenomenon reveals a critical truth: more data doesn't automatically translate to better business intelligence. In fact, accumulating vast quantities of unrefined, unstructured, or irrelevant data can actually hinder decision-making processes, drain resources, and create false confidence in flawed conclusions.

Understanding the Quality vs. Quantity Distinction

Data quantity refers to the sheer volume of information your organization collects and stores. Data quality, however, measures how fit that data is for its intended purpose. High-quality data possesses several essential characteristics:

  • Accuracy: The data correctly represents the real-world situation it's meant to describe
  • Completeness: All necessary data points are present without critical gaps
  • Consistency: Information remains uniform across different systems and databases
  • Timeliness: Data is current and available when needed for decision-making
  • Relevance: The information directly relates to your business objectives
  • Validity: Data conforms to defined business rules and formats

A manufacturing company tracking 50 essential performance metrics with 98% accuracy will generate far more valuable insights than one collecting 500 loosely defined data points with questionable reliability. The former enables confident strategic decisions; the latter creates analysis paralysis.

The Hidden Costs of Poor Data Quality

Low-quality data creates substantial financial and operational burdens that many organizations underestimate. According to Gartner research, poor data quality costs organizations an average of $12.9 million annually. These costs manifest in several ways:

Wasted Resources and Productivity Losses

Employees spend significant time cleaning, verifying, and reconciling inconsistent data rather than analyzing it. Data scientists report spending up to 60% of their time on data preparation tasks instead of generating insights. This represents a massive misallocation of skilled talent and expensive resources.

Flawed Decision-Making

When executives base strategies on inaccurate information, the consequences can be severe. Marketing campaigns targeting the wrong demographics, inventory decisions based on outdated demand data, and financial forecasts built on incomplete information all stem from quality problems rather than quantity shortfalls.

Customer Experience Degradation

Poor data quality directly impacts customer relationships. Duplicate records lead to communication errors, inaccurate customer information creates service friction, and inconsistent data across touchpoints damages trust. A single incorrect email address or outdated contact preference can end a customer relationship.

Compliance and Security Risks

Organizations handling inaccurate or improperly managed data face increased regulatory risks. GDPR, HIPAA, and other regulations require accurate, well-maintained records. Poor data quality can result in compliance violations, financial penalties, and reputational damage.

Why Organizations Prioritize Quantity Over Quality

Understanding why businesses fall into the quantity trap helps prevent it. Several factors contribute to this counterproductive pattern:

The "Big Data" Misconception: Marketing around big data technologies has created a perception that more data automatically yields better insights. This oversimplification ignores the critical importance of data governance and quality management.

Storage Cost Reduction: As cloud storage costs have plummeted, the financial barrier to hoarding data has disappeared. Organizations collect everything "just in case," without considering the downstream costs of managing that volume.

Fear of Missing Out: Decision-makers worry about lacking crucial information if they don't capture every possible data point. This defensive approach leads to undisciplined data collection strategies.

Technology-First Thinking: Investing in sophisticated analytics platforms before establishing data quality processes puts the cart before the horse. Even the most advanced AI algorithms produce unreliable results when fed poor-quality data.

Building a Quality-First Data Strategy

Shifting from a quantity-focused to a quality-focused data approach requires deliberate strategy and organizational commitment. The following framework helps businesses maximize the value of their information assets:

Define Clear Data Objectives

Start by identifying the specific business questions you need to answer. What decisions will this data inform? What outcomes are you trying to improve? This purpose-driven approach ensures you collect relevant, actionable information rather than accumulating data for its own sake.

Establish Data Governance Policies

Create clear ownership, standards, and processes for data management. Designate data stewards responsible for quality in their domains, define standardized formats and validation rules, and implement regular quality audits. Effective governance transforms data from a liability into a strategic asset.

Implement Validation at Collection Points

Preventing quality problems is more efficient than fixing them later. Build validation into data entry systems, automate quality checks where possible, and train employees on the importance of accurate data capture. A simple form field validation can prevent years of database cleanup work.

Prioritize Data Cleaning and Maintenance

Dedicate resources to identifying and correcting existing quality issues. This includes removing duplicates, filling critical gaps, standardizing formats, and archiving irrelevant information. While less glamorous than analytics projects, data cleaning delivers immediate ROI through improved decision quality.

Invest in the Right Technology Foundation

Modern data security and management solutions help organizations maintain quality at scale. The right infrastructure includes data quality monitoring tools, master data management systems, and automated validation processes that flag issues before they propagate through your systems.

How Technology Partners Support Data Quality

Many organizations lack the internal expertise or resources to transform their data management practices alone. Working with experienced technology partners can accelerate this transformation while avoiding common pitfalls.

Professional managed IT services provide the strategic guidance and technical capabilities needed to implement quality-first data strategies. These partnerships bring specialized knowledge in data architecture, governance frameworks, and quality monitoring systems that would take years to develop internally.

Additionally, cloud solutions offer scalable platforms with built-in data quality features. Modern cloud data warehouses include automated validation, lineage tracking, and quality dashboards that make maintaining high standards more manageable as data volumes grow.

Measuring and Monitoring Data Quality

You can't improve what you don't measure. Establish key performance indicators for data quality and track them consistently:

  • Error rates: Percentage of records containing inaccuracies or validation failures
  • Completeness scores: Proportion of required fields populated across critical datasets
  • Duplication rates: Number of redundant records in master data systems
  • Time to resolution: How quickly quality issues are identified and corrected
  • Data freshness: Average age of information in key operational systems

Regular quality reporting creates accountability and helps justify continued investment in data management capabilities.

Real-World Results: Quality Over Quantity Success Stories

Organizations that prioritize data quality over quantity consistently outperform their peers. A healthcare provider reduced patient identification errors by 94% after implementing strict data quality standards, directly improving patient safety outcomes.

A financial services firm decreased customer onboarding time by 40% by cleaning their client database and eliminating duplicate records. The improved data quality enabled automated processes that previously required manual review due to inconsistencies.

A manufacturing company improved demand forecasting accuracy by 28% not by collecting more data points, but by ensuring their existing sales, inventory, and market data met rigorous quality standards. This improvement reduced excess inventory costs and stockout incidents simultaneously.

Making the Shift: Your Next Steps

Transforming your organization's approach to data doesn't require a complete overhaul overnight. Start with these practical steps:

  1. Audit your current data assets to identify quality issues and their business impact
  2. Prioritize quality improvements in data sets that directly influence critical decisions
  3. Establish baseline quality metrics and set realistic improvement targets
  4. Train employees on why data quality matters and their role in maintaining it
  5. Implement technology solutions that automate quality monitoring and enforcement
  6. Review progress quarterly and adjust your approach based on results

The path to becoming a truly data-driven organization doesn't run through accumulating ever-larger data lakes. It requires a disciplined focus on quality, relevance, and actionability. By shifting your perspective from "How much data do we have?" to "How reliable is our data?", you'll unlock insights that actually move your business forward.

Ready to transform your data from a burden into a strategic advantage? Contact our team to discuss how we can help you implement a quality-first data strategy that delivers measurable business results.

title: Process Automation: Streamlining Operations for Growth
htmlTitle: Process Automation: Streamlining Operations for Growth
author: Van Ausdall & Farrar
teaser: Process automation has emerged as the solution that bridges this gap, transforming how organizations handle repetitive tasks and complex workflows. Learn more.
metaDescription: Process automation has emerged as the solution that bridges this gap, transforming how organizations handle repetitive tasks and complex workflows. Learn more.
bodyHtml:
The Business Case for Process Automation

Business operations today demand unprecedented efficiency. Organizations across manufacturing, healthcare, finance, and government sectors face mounting pressure to do more with less - serve more customers, process more transactions, and deliver faster results without proportionally increasing headcount or budgets. Process automation has emerged as the solution that bridges this gap, transforming how organizations handle repetitive tasks and complex workflows.

Process automation encompasses the technology-driven execution of recurring business activities, replacing manual effort with software-based systems. From invoice processing and document management to customer onboarding and compliance reporting, automation touches virtually every business function. According to recent research, organizations implementing process automation see an average 20-30% reduction in operational costs while improving accuracy rates to 99% or higher.

The value proposition extends beyond simple cost savings. Automation fundamentally reimagines how work gets done, freeing your team from tedious, error-prone manual tasks so they can focus on strategic initiatives that drive growth. When an accounts payable clerk spends hours manually entering invoice data, that's time lost that could be spent analyzing spending patterns or negotiating better vendor terms. Process automation reclaims that time.

Understanding Different Types of Process Automation

Document Processing and Management

Paper-based processes remain surprisingly common, even in organizations that consider themselves digitally mature. Document management automation transforms how businesses capture, process, store, and retrieve information. Intelligent document processing systems can automatically extract data from invoices, purchase orders, contracts, and forms - regardless of format - then route that information to appropriate systems and workflows.

Healthcare organizations leverage document automation to process patient intake forms, insurance claims, and medical records. Manufacturing companies automate quality control documentation and compliance reports. The technology adapts to various document types and learns over time, continuously improving accuracy.

Workflow Automation

Workflow automation orchestrates multi-step business processes that involve multiple stakeholders, systems, and decision points. Consider employee onboarding: a process that typically involves HR, IT, facilities, and department managers coordinating equipment provisioning, access rights, training schedules, and documentation. Workflow automation ensures each step happens in the right sequence, nothing falls through the cracks, and all parties receive appropriate notifications.

Financial services firms use workflow automation for loan approvals, moving applications through credit checks, underwriting, and approval stages with built-in compliance checkpoints. Insurance companies automate claims processing, dramatically reducing cycle times from weeks to days or even hours.

Robotic Process Automation (RPA)

Robotic Process Automation deploys software "bots" that mimic human interactions with digital systems. These bots can log into applications, copy and paste data between systems, perform calculations, generate reports, and execute other rule-based tasks. RPA excels at automating processes that span multiple systems that don't communicate directly - a common challenge in organizations with legacy technology stacks.

A logistics company might use RPA to automatically update shipment tracking information across customer portals, internal systems, and partner platforms. Accounting departments deploy bots for month-end closing procedures, automatically gathering data from various sources and populating consolidated reports.

Intelligent Automation and AI Integration

The next frontier combines traditional process automation with artificial intelligence capabilities. Machine learning algorithms can handle unstructured data, make contextual decisions, and continuously improve performance. This enables automation of processes previously considered too complex or variable for traditional automation approaches.

Customer service operations use AI-powered chatbots that understand natural language, answer questions, and handle routine requests without human intervention. Supply chain operations leverage predictive analytics to automatically adjust inventory levels and reorder points based on demand forecasting.

Identifying Automation Opportunities in Your Organization

Not every process makes a good automation candidate. The highest-value opportunities typically share several characteristics:

  • High volume: Processes performed frequently deliver greater returns on automation investment
  • Rule-based: Tasks that follow predictable logic and decision trees automate more easily
  • Error-prone: Manual processes with high error rates benefit dramatically from automation's consistency
  • Time-sensitive: Processes with strict timing requirements or SLAs gain reliability through automation
  • Compliance-critical: Activities requiring audit trails and regulatory documentation benefit from automation's built-in tracking

Start by mapping current workflows across departments. Engage team members who actually perform the work - they understand pain points and inefficiencies that may not be visible to management. Look for bottlenecks where work queues up, handoffs between departments that involve delays, and tasks that people describe as tedious or frustrating.

Manufacturing and logistics operations often find excellent automation opportunities in inventory management, quality assurance documentation, and shipping coordination. Healthcare organizations typically see quick wins in patient scheduling, billing processes, and medical records management. Government agencies benefit from automating permit applications, citizen request processing, and reporting workflows.

Implementing Process Automation: Best Practices

Start Small, Think Big

Successful automation initiatives begin with pilot projects rather than organization-wide transformations. Select a well-defined process with clear success metrics, implement automation, measure results, and learn from the experience. This approach builds organizational confidence, develops internal expertise, and provides concrete ROI data that justifies broader investment.

A regional insurance company might start by automating policy renewal processing before expanding to new policy applications and claims handling. An engineering firm could begin with automated timesheet processing before tackling project resource allocation and billing workflows.

Optimize Before You Automate

Automation codifies existing processes - if those processes are inefficient, automation simply performs inefficient work faster. Before implementing automation, critically examine current workflows. Eliminate unnecessary steps, streamline handoffs, and clarify decision criteria. Process optimization followed by automation delivers exponentially better results than automation alone.

Ensure Data Quality and Integration

Process automation depends on accurate, accessible data. Assess the quality of data in your existing systems and establish governance practices that maintain data integrity. Automated processes that rely on incomplete, inconsistent, or outdated data will produce unreliable results that undermine confidence in the technology.

Integration between systems presents another critical consideration. Cloud solutions and modern integration platforms simplify connecting disparate systems, but planning the data flow between applications requires careful attention to field mapping, validation rules, and error handling.

Plan for Change Management

Process automation changes how people work, which naturally creates resistance. Communicate clearly about automation's purpose - emphasize that technology augments human capabilities rather than replacing people. Involve team members in implementation, provide comprehensive training, and celebrate early wins. Organizations that manage the human side of automation carefully see much higher adoption rates and better outcomes.

Measuring Automation Success

Establishing clear metrics enables you to track automation value and identify improvement opportunities. Key performance indicators vary by process but often include:

  • Cycle time reduction: How much faster does the automated process complete compared to manual execution?
  • Error rates: What percentage of transactions complete without requiring human intervention or correction?
  • Cost per transaction: What does each process execution cost after automation compared to before?
  • Processing capacity: How many more transactions can you handle with the same resources?
  • Employee satisfaction: Are team members more engaged now that they're freed from repetitive tasks?

Calculate both hard savings (reduced labor hours, lower error correction costs) and soft benefits (faster customer service, improved compliance, better employee retention). A comprehensive view of automation impact helps justify continued investment and guides decisions about which processes to automate next.

Security and Compliance Considerations

Automated processes often handle sensitive data and business-critical operations, making security paramount. Implement robust access controls ensuring only authorized systems and users can trigger automated workflows or access processing data. Maintain comprehensive audit logs documenting every automated action for compliance reporting and troubleshooting.

Industry-specific regulations shape automation requirements. Healthcare organizations must ensure business process solutions comply with HIPAA privacy and security rules. Financial services firms need to meet SOX requirements for financial reporting controls. Government agencies must adhere to public records laws and accessibility standards.

Working with experienced technology partners helps navigate these compliance requirements and implement automation that meets regulatory standards while delivering operational benefits.

The Future of Process Automation

Process automation continues evolving rapidly. Artificial intelligence and machine learning expand the scope of what can be automated, handling increasingly complex, judgment-based tasks. Low-code and no-code automation platforms democratize automation development, enabling business users to create automated workflows without extensive programming knowledge.

Hyperautomation - the coordinated use of multiple automation technologies including RPA, AI, workflow orchestration, and integration platforms - represents the next maturity level. Organizations pursuing hyperautomation strategies see the most transformative results, fundamentally reimagining operations rather than simply automating isolated tasks.

Taking the Next Step

Process automation delivers measurable value across industries and business functions. Whether you're looking to reduce operational costs, improve service delivery, enhance compliance, or free your team for more strategic work, automation provides a clear path forward.

The key to success lies in approaching automation strategically - identifying the right processes, implementing thoughtfully, managing change effectively, and measuring results consistently. Organizations that treat automation as an ongoing capability rather than a one-time project see the greatest long-term benefits.

If you're ready to explore how process automation can transform your operations, contact our team for a consultation. We'll assess your current processes, identify high-value automation opportunities, and develop a roadmap that aligns with your business goals and technical environment. With over a century of experience helping organizations optimize their operations through technology, we bring the expertise needed to ensure your automation initiatives deliver real results.

title: AI Readiness: Governance Comes Before the Tools
htmlTitle: AI Readiness: Governance Comes Before the Tools
author: Van Ausdall & Farrar
featuredImageAlt: AI governance panel discussion at the Valve+Meter masterclass in Indianapolis
teaser: AI readiness starts with governance, not tools. What Steven Sigmon shared on an Indianapolis panel about acceptable use, data governance, and shadow AI risk.
metaDescription: AI readiness starts with governance, not tools. What Steven Sigmon shared on an Indianapolis panel about acceptable use, data governance, and shadow AI risk.
bodyHtml:
On August 26, Steven Sigmon, Director of IT at Van Ausdall & Farrar, took the panel stage at the AI & Marketing Masterclass at Ruth's Chris in Indianapolis. Presented by Valve+Meter Performance Marketing alongside Van Ausdall & Farrar and Leaf Software Solutions, the invite-only session drew manufacturers, distributors, and logistics teams, the businesses most likely to be handed an AI tool and told to find something useful to do with it.

The panel's theme was AI usage, governance, and safety. The message that kept surfacing was that the tool is the easy part.

Readiness Comes Before Tools

Most AI conversations start with a product. Sigmon starts somewhere else. “What is the business problem that we're trying to solve, what's the friction, what's the repeatable process that we're trying to utilize AI to help with,” he said. “It's really understanding the problem before we just throw tools out there to fix.”

That order matters. A tool chosen before the problem is defined produces a pilot that never reaches production, or one that quietly becomes a second way of doing the same work. The question worth asking first is which process is repetitive, rules-based, and expensive enough that shaving time off it justifies a project.

What an Acceptable Use Policy Actually Covers

Sigmon's more pointed question was about readiness. “Is there an AI policy? Do we need to help out with an AI policy? Do we have guardrails with AI and what we're using?”

An acceptable use policy is neither a ban nor a permission slip. It answers the questions your team is already improvising answers to:

  • Which tools are approved, and which are prohibited outright
  • What categories of data may be entered into an approved tool : and what may never be
  • Whether vendor training on your inputs is on or off, and how that gets verified
  • Who reviews a new AI tool before someone starts using one
  • How outputs are checked before they reach a customer, a contract, or a filing
  • What happens when something goes wrong

Written down, that is a page or two. Unwritten, the policy still exists, it is just different in every employee's head.

Shadow AI Is a Data Governance Problem

The risk the panel kept returning to is not that employees use AI. It is that they use it with company data, in tools nobody vetted, and no one finds out until a client asks a question.

Consider what leaves the building when someone pastes a spreadsheet into a consumer chatbot to clean it up: customer names, pricing, contract terms, employee records. The employee's goal is reasonable, they are trying to finish faster, which is exactly why a ban does not hold. People route around a rule that blocks the work.

Data governance solves it from the other direction. Classify what you hold, decide which classifications may enter which tools, and then give people an approved path to the same outcome so the honest option is also the fast one. Businesses that already take document management seriously have most of this groundwork done, they know where their sensitive data lives.

Where the Guardrails Come From

Governance for AI is less a new discipline than a familiar one applied to a new tool. The controls that protect the rest of your environment carry over: identity, access, data classification, monitoring, and a plan for when something slips through.

That is why AI readiness tends to stall in organizations missing a foundation. If nobody owns network security, nobody owns the AI guardrails either. Van Ausdall & Farrar's AI consulting work starts with the acceptable use framework and the governance questions above, then builds outward to tooling, the reverse of how most AI projects begin. It is a natural extension of the managed IT services we already deliver, because the team watching your environment is the team that decides what may connect to it.

A Readiness Check Takes an Afternoon

You do not need a committee or a twelve-month roadmap to find out where you stand. Four questions get most of the way:

  1. Which AI tools are your employees using today, and how do you know?
  2. What company data have they put into them?
  3. Is there a written policy, and does anyone remember reading it?
  4. Who decides whether the next tool is allowed?

If any answer is “we're not sure,” that is the finding. Not a failure, a starting point, and a far cheaper one to reach now than after an incident.

AI readiness is a short engagement, not a long one. Schedule a Technology Strength Assessment and we will review your data handling and give you a straight read on what has to be in place before the tools go out.

title: Modern Communication Systems: Transforming Business Connectivity
htmlTitle: Modern Communication Systems for Business Connectivity
author: Van Ausdall & Farrar
teaser: Business communication has undergone a dramatic transformation over the past decade. Talk to our specialists today to find the right solution for your business.
metaDescription: Business communication has undergone a dramatic transformation over the past decade. Talk to our specialists today to find the right solution for your business.
bodyHtml:
The Evolution of Business Communication Systems

Business communication has undergone a dramatic transformation over the past decade. Organizations that once relied solely on traditional phone systems now have access to sophisticated, integrated communication platforms that connect teams across locations, enable seamless collaboration, and deliver superior customer experiences. Understanding these modern communication systems and their strategic implementation is essential for businesses seeking competitive advantages in an increasingly connected marketplace.

The shift from legacy PBX systems to cloud-based unified communications represents more than just a technology upgrade - it's a fundamental reimagining of how organizations connect internally and externally. With 70% of businesses now adopting some form of cloud communication technology, according to recent industry research, the question is no longer whether to modernize but how to do so strategically and effectively.

Understanding Unified Communications

Unified communications (UC) integrates multiple communication tools into a single, cohesive platform. Rather than managing separate systems for voice calls, video conferencing, instant messaging, and email, UC consolidates these functions, creating a streamlined experience that enhances productivity and reduces complexity.

Core Components of Modern Communication Systems

  • Voice over IP (VoIP): Cloud-based phone systems that transmit calls over internet connections, eliminating the need for traditional phone lines and enabling advanced features like call routing, voicemail-to-email, and mobile integration
  • Video Conferencing: High-definition video meetings that support remote collaboration, reducing travel costs while maintaining face-to-face interaction
  • Instant Messaging and Presence: Real-time chat capabilities with presence indicators that show colleague availability, enabling quick questions and reducing email overload
  • File Sharing and Collaboration: Integrated document sharing and co-editing features that facilitate teamwork across locations
  • Mobile Integration: Seamless access to all communication tools from smartphones and tablets, supporting flexible work arrangements

These components work together to create a communication ecosystem that adapts to how people actually work, rather than forcing workflows to accommodate technology limitations.

Business Benefits of Modern Communication Systems

Cost Reduction and Operational Efficiency

Organizations implementing cloud communications typically realize significant cost savings. Traditional phone systems require substantial upfront capital investment in hardware, ongoing maintenance contracts, and expensive upgrades every few years. Cloud-based systems operate on a predictable subscription model with no hardware to maintain on-premises.

A mid-sized organization with 150 employees can save between $50,000 and $100,000 annually by transitioning from legacy phone systems to cloud-based alternatives. These savings come from reduced equipment costs, lower maintenance expenses, elimination of separate data and voice networks, and decreased telecom charges - especially for long-distance and international calls.

Enhanced Collaboration and Productivity

When communication tools are fragmented, employees waste valuable time switching between applications, searching for information, and coordinating across platforms. Unified systems eliminate these inefficiencies. Studies show that integrated communication platforms can improve employee productivity by 20-25% by reducing the time spent on communication logistics.

Consider a typical scenario: A sales representative needs to quickly consult with an engineer about a client question. With unified communications, they can instantly see if the engineer is available, send a quick message or initiate a video call, share relevant documents in real-time, and resolve the issue - all within minutes and without leaving their primary workspace.

Superior Customer Experience

Modern business phone systems dramatically improve customer interactions. Advanced call routing ensures customers reach the right person quickly. Integration with CRM systems provides representatives with complete customer history before answering calls. Call recording and quality monitoring enable continuous service improvement.

Organizations that implement comprehensive communication systems report 35% improvements in first-call resolution rates and significant increases in customer satisfaction scores. These improvements directly impact revenue, as satisfied customers exhibit higher retention rates and lifetime value.

Key Technologies Driving Communication Innovation

Cloud Infrastructure

Cloud technology forms the foundation of modern communication systems. Cloud-based platforms offer scalability that traditional systems cannot match - adding users, features, or capacity requires simple configuration changes rather than hardware installations. This flexibility is particularly valuable for growing organizations or those with seasonal staffing fluctuations.

Cloud systems also provide geographic redundancy and disaster recovery capabilities. If a local internet connection fails, calls automatically route to mobile devices or alternate locations, ensuring business continuity. This resilience would require substantial investment in redundant hardware with traditional systems.

Artificial Intelligence Integration

Artificial intelligence is transforming communication systems from passive tools to active productivity enhancers. AI-powered features include:

  • Intelligent call routing that directs customers to the best-qualified representative based on skills, availability, and caller history
  • Real-time transcription and translation services that break down language barriers
  • Sentiment analysis that alerts supervisors when customers express frustration
  • Automated meeting summaries and action item extraction
  • Virtual assistants that handle routine inquiries without human intervention

These AI capabilities are becoming standard features rather than premium add-ons, making sophisticated communication intelligence accessible to organizations of all sizes.

Software-Defined Wide Area Networks (SD-WAN)

Quality of service is critical for voice and video communications. SD-WAN technology intelligently manages network traffic, prioritizing real-time communications over less time-sensitive data transfers. This ensures clear, uninterrupted calls even when networks are under heavy load.

SD-WAN also enables organizations to use multiple internet connections simultaneously, improving reliability and bandwidth while reducing costs compared to traditional dedicated voice circuits.

Implementation Considerations for Communication System Upgrades

Assessing Current Infrastructure

Successful communication system implementations begin with thorough assessment of existing infrastructure. Organizations should evaluate current bandwidth capacity, network reliability, internal IT capabilities, and specific business requirements. Understanding baseline capabilities and identifying gaps ensures the new system will perform optimally from day one.

A comprehensive managed IT services provider can conduct detailed assessments that identify potential issues before they impact deployment, ensuring smooth transitions with minimal disruption.

Change Management and User Adoption

Technology is only valuable when people use it effectively. Successful implementations include comprehensive training programs, clear communication about benefits and changes, ongoing support during the transition period, and champions who advocate for the new system within teams.

Organizations should plan for a transition period where both old and new systems operate simultaneously, allowing users to become comfortable with new tools without losing access to familiar capabilities.

Security and Compliance

Modern communication systems must meet stringent security and compliance requirements, particularly for organizations in healthcare, finance, and government sectors. Key security considerations include end-to-end encryption for all communications, secure access controls and authentication, compliance with industry regulations like HIPAA or PCI-DSS, and regular security audits and updates.

Partnering with experienced providers ensures communication systems meet all necessary security standards while maintaining usability and performance.

Industry-Specific Communication Solutions

Different industries have unique communication requirements. Healthcare organizations need HIPAA-compliant systems with secure messaging for patient information. Financial services require recorded lines and audit trails for regulatory compliance. Educational institutions benefit from communication tools that integrate with learning management systems and support hybrid teaching models.

Modern communication platforms offer industry-specific configurations and integrations that address these specialized needs without requiring custom development or complex workarounds.

The Future of Business Communications

Communication technology continues to evolve rapidly. Emerging trends include deeper integration with business applications, creating seamless workflows across all business systems. Enhanced video capabilities with features like virtual backgrounds, noise cancellation, and AI-powered framing are becoming standard. Advanced analytics provide insights into communication patterns, helping organizations optimize processes and identify training opportunities.

Organizations that proactively adopt modern communication systems position themselves to take advantage of these innovations as they emerge, maintaining competitive advantages through superior connectivity and collaboration capabilities.

Taking the Next Step

Upgrading communication systems represents a strategic investment in organizational capability. The benefits - reduced costs, improved productivity, enhanced customer experiences, and greater flexibility - deliver measurable returns that justify the transition effort.

Organizations beginning this journey should start with clear objectives, assess current capabilities honestly, engage experienced implementation partners, and plan for comprehensive training and support. With proper planning and execution, modern communication systems become powerful enablers of business success.

Van Ausdall & Farrar has helped hundreds of Midwest organizations successfully transition to modern communication platforms. Our century of technology experience, combined with deep expertise in unified communications and business process optimization, ensures implementations that deliver promised benefits while minimizing disruption. Contact our team to discuss how advanced communication systems can transform your organization's connectivity and collaboration capabilities.
